[{"order":1,"type":"heading","text":"Cloud Datastore: NoSQL Document Database on Google Cloud"},{"order":2,"type":"paragraph","text":"Cloud Datastore, now known as Datastore mode in Firestore, is a highly scalable NoSQL document database provided by Google Cloud Platform (GCP). It's designed for automatically managing the scaling and sharding of your data, allowing developers to focus on building applications rather than database administration. This tutorial will guide you through the fundamentals of Cloud Datastore and how to use it effectively."},{"order":3,"type":"subheading","text":"Key Features of Cloud Datastore"},{"order":4,"type":"bullet_point","text":"Scalability: Datastore automatically scales to handle increasing data volumes and read/write loads."},{"order":5,"type":"bullet_point","text":"Schema-less: Datastore is schema-less, meaning you don't need to define a fixed schema for your data. Each entity can have its own set of properties."},{"order":6,"type":"bullet_point","text":"ACID Transactions: Datastore supports ACID (Atomicity, Consistency, Isolation, Durability) transactions, ensuring data integrity."},{"order":7,"type":"bullet_point","text":"Indexing: Datastore provides automatic and manual indexing to optimize query performance."},{"order":8,"type":"bullet_point","text":"Strong Consistency: Datastore offers strong consistency for ancestor queries and eventual consistency for global queries."},{"order":9,"type":"subheading","text":"Setting up Cloud Datastore"},{"order":10,"type":"paragraph","text":"Before you can use Cloud Datastore, you need a Google Cloud project. If you don't have one, create a new project in the Google Cloud Console. Once you have a project, enable the Datastore API."},{"order":11,"type":"paragraph","text":"1. Go to the Google Cloud Console: console.cloud.google.com"},{"order":12,"type":"paragraph","text":"2. Select your project."},{"order":13,"type":"paragraph","text":"3. Navigate to 'Firestore' (Datastore mode)."},{"order":14,"type":"paragraph","text":"4. Select a location for your Datastore database. This location cannot be changed later."},{"order":15,"type":"subheading","text":"Data Model: Entities, Properties, and Keys"},{"order":16,"type":"paragraph","text":"Datastore stores data as entities. An entity is a data object with one or more properties. Each entity has a key, which uniquely identifies it."},{"order":17,"type":"bullet_point","text":"Entity: A data object (e.g., a user, a product, a blog post)."},{"order":18,"type":"bullet_point","text":"Property: An attribute of an entity (e.g., a user's name, a product's price, a blog post's title)."},{"order":19,"type":"bullet_point","text":"Key: A unique identifier for an entity. It consists of a kind and an ID or name."},{"order":20,"type":"subheading","text":"Writing Data to Datastore"},{"order":21,"type":"paragraph","text":"Here's an example of how to write data to Datastore using the Python client library:"},{"order":22,"type":"code","text":"from google.cloud import datastore

# Instantiate a client.
client = datastore.Client()

# The kind for the new entity
kind = 'Task'
# The name/ID for the new entity
name = 'sampletask'
# The Cloud Datastore key for the new entity
task_key = client.key(kind, name)

# Prepares the new entity
task = datastore.Entity(key=task_key)
task['description'] = 'Buy milk'

# Saves the entity
client.put(task)

print(f'Saved {task.key.name}: {task["description"]}')"},{"order":23,"type":"subheading","text":"Reading Data from Datastore"},{"order":24,"type":"paragraph","text":"To read data from Datastore, you can use queries. Here's an example:"},{"order":25,"type":"code","text":"from google.cloud import datastore

# Instantiate a client
client = datastore.Client()

# Construct a query
query = client.query(kind='Task')
query.add_filter('description', '=', 'Buy milk')

# Fetch the results
results = list(query.fetch())

for entity in results:
    print(f'Task: {entity["description"]}')"},{"order":26,"type":"subheading","text":"Transactions"},{"order":27,"type":"paragraph","text":"Datastore supports transactions to ensure data consistency. A transaction is a set of operations that either all succeed or all fail. Here's an example:"},{"order":28,"type":"code","text":"from google.cloud import datastore

client = datastore.Client()

def update_counter(counter_name):
    key = client.key('Counter', counter_name)

    @client.transactional()
    def increment():
        entity = client.get(key)

        if not entity:
            entity = datastore.Entity(key)
            entity['count'] = 0

        entity['count'] += 1
        client.put(entity)

    increment()

update_counter('my_counter')"},{"order":29,"type":"subheading","text":"Indexing"},{"order":30,"type":"paragraph","text":"Datastore uses indexes to efficiently execute queries. Datastore automatically creates indexes for simple queries. For more complex queries, you may need to define custom indexes in the index.yaml file. This file is uploaded to Datastore to create the necessary indexes."},{"order":31,"type":"subheading","text":"Best Practices"},{"order":32,"type":"bullet_point","text":"Use keys effectively: Design your keys to optimize query performance."},{"order":33,"type":"bullet_point","text":"Avoid large entities: Break down large entities into smaller ones to improve performance."},{"order":34,"type":"bullet_point","text":"Use transactions wisely: Use transactions only when necessary to maintain data consistency."},{"order":35,"type":"bullet_point","text":"Monitor performance: Regularly monitor Datastore performance and optimize queries as needed."},{"order":36,"type":"subheading","text":"Conclusion"},{"order":37,"type":"paragraph","text":"Cloud Datastore is a powerful NoSQL document database that offers scalability, flexibility, and ease of use. By understanding its key features and following best practices, you can effectively use Datastore to build scalable and reliable applications on Google Cloud Platform."}]
